Back: FTP Data - File Transfer Protocol data transfer channel. Unencrypted file transfer. Security risk: credentials and files sent in plaintext. Prefer SFTP (port 22) or FTPS (port 990).

FTP Control - File Transfer Protocol command/control channel. Unencrypted. Security risk: plaintext credentials. Exam tip: FTP active uses server connecting back to client on random port; passive uses server-range ports.
SSH - Secure Shell. Encrypted remote administration, file transfer (SCP/SFTP), port forwarding. Replaces insecure Telnet (port 23). Key security tool for Linux/network device management.
Telnet - Unencrypted remote terminal access. All data including credentials sent in cleartext. Deprecated/retired from most modern environments. Exam expects: identify as insecure, replace with SSH.

SMTP - Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. Used for email transmission between mail servers (MTA-to-MTA). Unencrypted by default. Often blocked by ISPs to prevent spam relay. Secured via STARTTLS on port 587.

DNS - Domain Name System. Converts hostnames to IP addresses. UDP for standard queries (fast, connectionless). TCP for zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) and responses exceeding 512 bytes. Security: DNSSEC validates response integrity; DNS poisoning/spoofing are exam-critical attacks.

DHCP Server - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server port. Listens for client discovery messages (DHCPDISCOVER) and offers IP configuration. Security: rogue DHCP servers can perform MITM; use DHCP snooping on switches.
DHCP Client - Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol client port. Client sends/receives on this port during DORA process (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge).

TFTP - Trivial File Transfer Protocol. No authentication, no encryption. Used for network device backups, firmware updates, PXE boot. Security risk: no access control; restrict with ACLs. Exam: lightweight but insecure.
HTTP - Hypertext Transfer Protocol. Unencrypted web traffic. All data in cleartext. Security: use HTTPS (port 443) with TLS. Modern browsers mark HTTP sites as 'Not Secure'.

Kerberos - Network authentication protocol using tickets/ticket-granting tickets (TGT). Used by Active Directory. Provides mutual authentication. Single sign-on (SSO) enabled. Port 88 is the Kerberos authentication service.
POP3 - Post Office Protocol v3. Retrieves email from server to client (download-and-delete model). Unencrypted. Replaced by POP3S (port 995) with TLS. Does NOT sync across multiple devices.

NTP - Network Time Protocol. Synchronizes system clocks across networks. Critical for security logging (accurate timestamps), Kerberos authentication (time skew tolerance), and certificate validation. NTP amplification used in DDoS attacks.

MS-RPC - Microsoft Remote Procedure Call. Used for Windows network services (DCOM, WMI). Common attack vector historically (Blaster worm). Often filtered at network perimeter. Security: restrict with Windows Firewall.

NetBIOS Name Service - Part of legacy NetBIOS over TCP/IP (NBT). Resolves NetBIOS names to IP addresses. Known as NBNS. Insecure, frequently targeted for spoofing. Disable in modern Windows environments.
NetBIOS Datagram Service - NetBIOS datagram transport. Used for connectionless NetBIOS communication. Legacy protocol, security risk. Block at firewall in modern networks.
NetBIOS Session Service - NetBIOS session establishment. Used for file/print sharing in legacy Windows networks. Replaced by SMB over port 445 (direct SMB without NetBIOS).
IMAP - Internet Message Access Protocol. Email retrieval that keeps messages on server. Supports folders, server-side search, multi-device sync. Unencrypted. Replaced by IMAPS (port 993).

SNMP - Simple Network Management Protocol agent port (queries). Network device monitoring (routers, switches, printers, servers). Versions: v1/v2c use community strings (plaintext 'password'), insecure. v3 adds encryption and authentication. Security: change default community strings 'public'/'private'.
SNMP Trap - SNMP asynchronous alert notifications. Managed devices send traps (events) to the NMS (Network Management Station) on this port. Examples: interface down, high CPU, temperature threshold.

BGP - Border Gateway Protocol. Exterior gateway protocol routing the internet. Exchanges routing information between autonomous systems (AS). Uses TCP for reliable peering. Security: BGP hijacking is a critical attack vector; use RPKI/ROA for validation.

LDAP - Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Accesses and maintains directory services (Active Directory, OpenLDAP). Queries user objects, groups, computers. Unencrypted; replaced by LDAPS (port 636).

HTTPS - HTTP over TLS. Encrypted web traffic. Uses TLS (SSL successor) for confidentiality and integrity. The cornerstone of web security. Exam: know TLS handshake, certificate validation, cipher suites.

SMB - Server Message Block (direct). Windows file and printer sharing, named pipes, remote administration. Eliminates NetBIOS dependency (port 139). Security: EternalBlue exploit (WannaCry 2017) used SMBv1; disable SMBv1, use SMBv3 with encryption.

ISAKMP/IKE - Internet Security Association and Key Management Protocol / Internet Key Exchange. Used for IPsec VPN negotiation. Establishes Security Associations (SAs) and exchanges cryptographic keys (IKE phase 1).

Syslog - System logging protocol. Sends log messages from network devices to a centralized syslog server. Unencrypted; can leak sensitive data. Use Syslog over TLS (port 6514) for secure transport. Standard log format: facility, severity, timestamp, hostname, message.

SMTP Submission - Email submission from mail clients (MUA) to mail server (MSA). Requires authentication and supports STARTTLS for encryption. Replaces port 25 for client submission. Exam: recognize port 587 for authenticated/sending email.
LDAPS - LDAP over TLS/SSL. Secure directory service queries. Encrypts LDAP communication. Uses port 636 for global. Exam tip: domain controllers also listen on 3269 for Global Catalog LDAPS.
IMAPS - IMAP over TLS/SSL. Secure email retrieval with encryption. Keeps email on server (like IMAP) but encrypted in transit. Supports multi-device sync, folders, server-side search.
POP3S - POP3 over TLS/SSL. Secure email retrieval. Downloads email and encrypts transit. Typically deletes from server (download-and-delete model). No multi-device sync.

OpenVPN - Open-source VPN protocol. Highly configurable, runs on custom port (default 1194). Can use TCP (for reliability) or UDP (for performance). Uses TLS for control channel, supports various ciphers and auth methods.

MSSQL - Microsoft SQL Server database. Default port for SQL Server database engine. Security: restrict with firewall, use encrypted connections, disable sa account, use least-privilege service accounts.

RADIUS Authentication (legacy) - Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service. Legacy port for RADIUS authentication (RFC 2138/2865). IANA assigned 1812 as the standard port, but 1645 is widely used in legacy Cisco/Juniper environments.
RADIUS Accounting (legacy) - Legacy port for RADIUS accounting messages (start/stop/update). IANA assigned 1813 as standard. Many network devices use 1645/1646 instead of 1812/1813.
L2TP - Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol. VPN tunneling protocol that provides no encryption on its own. Typically combined with IPsec (L2TP/IPsec) for encryption. Commonly used with PPTP's successor.

PPTP - Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol. Legacy VPN protocol from Microsoft. Uses MPPE for encryption (considered broken/insecure). Deprecated in favor of L2TP/IPsec, SSTP, or IKEv2. Security: known vulnerabilities, avoid on exam.

RADIUS Authentication - Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (standard port 1812 by IANA). Centralized AAA for network devices (802.1X, VPN, WPA-Enterprise). Uses shared secret (no encryption of full packet, only password is encrypted). Exam: know RADIUS ports 1812/1813 for AAA.
RADIUS Accounting - RADIUS accounting standard port. Tracks user session start/stop, data usage, duration. Critical for billing, auditing, and usage tracking. Sent asynchronously from authentication.

Docker (unencrypted) - Docker REST API without TLS. Exposes Docker daemon over network. Security risk: anyone with API access can run containers (including root). Never expose to untrusted networks. Use port 2376 with TLS.
Docker (TLS) - Docker REST API with TLS encryption. Secure way to expose Docker daemon remotely. Requires client and server certificates. Exam: know 2375 (insecure) vs 2376 (secure) distinction.

Global Catalog (LDAP) - Microsoft Active Directory Global Catalog. Queries across all domains in a forest (forest-wide searches). Non-secure LDAP on port 3268. Used when search scope needs to span domains.
Global Catalog (LDAPS) - Microsoft Active Directory Global Catalog over TLS. Secure forest-wide directory queries. Encrypted version of port 3268.

MySQL / MariaDB - Open-source relational database. Default port for MySQL and its fork MariaDB. Security: bind to 127.0.0.1 if local-only, use strong passwords, avoid root remote login, use SSL/TLS connections.

RDP - Remote Desktop Protocol. Microsoft remote GUI access to Windows systems. UDP improves performance. Security: major attack surface (BlueKeep CVE-2019-0708); use VPN, Network Level Authentication (NLA), restrict via firewall, enable account lockout.

IPsec NAT-T - IPsec Network Address Translation Traversal. Allows IPsec ESP packets to pass through NAT devices. NAT breaks AH/ESP; NAT-T encapsulates IPsec in UDP port 4500. Used when both peers are behind NAT.
PostgreSQL - Advanced open-source relational database. Default port for Postgres. Security: use pg_hba.conf for host-based auth, require SSL, avoid default 'postgres' superuser remote access.

VNC - Virtual Network Computing. Cross-platform remote desktop/display sharing (RFB protocol). Security: typically unencrypted (no native encryption); tunnel through SSH or use VPN. Replace with SSH X forwarding or RDP with NLA.

WinRM HTTP - Windows Remote Management over HTTP. PowerShell remoting, WS-Management protocol. Uses HTTP (unencrypted by default). Security: prefer port 5986 with HTTPS. Microsoft management tools rely on WinRM.

WinRM HTTPS - Windows Remote Management over HTTPS. Encrypted PowerShell remoting and remote management. Uses TLS. Replaces DCOM/PSExec for remote Windows administration. Exam: know 5985 (HTTP) vs 5986 (HTTPS).

Kubernetes API Server - kube-apiserver. Primary management entrypoint for Kubernetes clusters. All kubectl commands, pod deployments, and cluster operations hit this API. Security: requires TLS client cert or token authentication, RBAC authorization.
Syslog over TLS - Reliable and encrypted syslog message transport. Uses TCP with TLS for confidentiality/integrity. Defined in RFC 5425. Replaces plain UDP syslog (port 514) for secure logging.

HTTP Alternate - Common alternate HTTP port. Used for web proxies, application servers (Tomcat, Jenkins), development servers, and caching proxies. Security: often misconfigured, inadvertently exposed. Not encrypted by default.
HTTPS Alternate - Common alternate HTTPS port. Used for application servers, web consoles (VMware vCenter, JBoss, Tomcat admin), and dev/staging environments. Uses TLS.

MongoDB - NoSQL document database. Default MongoDB daemon (mongod) port. Security: major ransomware target; bind to localhost, enable authentication, use TLS, avoid default ports for production (security through obscurity as a layer).

TACACS+ - Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus. Cisco proprietary AAA protocol. Encrypts entire packet (not just password like RADIUS). Separates authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA). Uses TCP for reliability.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): connection-oriented, reliable delivery, sequencing/ordering, error checking, flow control, retransmission. UDP (User Datagram Protocol): connectionless, no reliability guarantee, faster/lower overhead, no sequencing. Exam: TCP for web/email/file transfer; UDP for DNS/DHCP/streaming/ VoIP.

Transport Mode: encrypts only payload (original IP header intact). Used for end-to-end communication between two hosts. Tunnel Mode: encrypts entire original packet and adds new IP header. Used for VPN gateways (site-to-site). Exam: Transport = host-to-host; Tunnel = gateway-to-gateway or host-to-gateway.

AH (Authentication Header): provides integrity and authentication only, no encryption. Protects entire packet including IP header. Protocol 51. ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload): provides confidentiality (encryption), integrity, and authentication. Only protects IP payload (inner packet in tunnel mode). Protocol 50. Exam: Use ESP (provides encryption, AH doesn't).

TLS (Transport Layer Security): operates over TCP. Requires reliable transport. Standard for HTTPS, SMTPS, etc. DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security): operates over UDP. Designed for latency-sensitive/real-time apps (VoIP, video streaming, IoT). Based on TLS with modifications for datagram loss/reordering. Exam: DTLS is TLS over UDP.

DNS Security Extensions. Adds cryptographic validation to DNS responses. Uses digital signatures (RRSIG records) to verify response authenticity and integrity. Prevents DNS spoofing/cache poisoning. Does NOT encrypt queries. Exam: DNSSEC signs, does not encrypt.

Secure Access Service Edge (Gartner). Converges networking and security in the cloud. Components: SD-WAN, SWG (Secure Web Gateway), CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker), ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access), FWaaS (Firewall as a Service), DNS security, DLP. Exam: SASE = networking + security from cloud.

Traditional WAN: MPLS circuits, backhaul traffic to data center for security inspection, rigid, expensive. SD-WAN: software-defined, uses broadband/internet links, intelligent path selection, application-aware routing, integrates with cloud security (SASE), lower cost. Exam: SD-WAN is more flexible, cost-effective, cloud-integrated.

IP Protocol 49 (not port) - IPsec Authentication Header (AH). Provides connectionless integrity, data origin authentication, and anti-replay for IP packets. Does not provide encryption. See AH vs ESP card for details.

IP Protocol 50 (not port) - IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). Provides encryption, authentication, integrity, and anti-replay for IP packets. Most common IPsec protocol. Can be used in transport or tunnel mode.

IP Protocol 51 (not port) - IPsec Authentication Header (AH). Same as protocol 49 (AH). Ensures data integrity and authentication but no encryption. Not commonly used; ESP with null encryption is preferred when only authentication is needed.

QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections) - HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP (not TCP). Provides TLS 1.3 built-in, 0-RTT connection establishment, multiplexed streams without head-of-line blocking. Uses port 443 and looks like UDP to firewalls. Exam: QUIC = UDP-based, faster than TCP+TLS, HTTP/3 protocol.
LDAPS - LDAP over TLS/SSL. Secure directory queries. Encrypts all LDAP traffic. Uses separate port (636) rather than STARTTLS on port 389. Standard for modern AD/LDAP environments.
Global Catalog (LDAP) - Active Directory Global Catalog. LDAP port for queries across all domains in forest. Used when searching for objects beyond a single domain. Unencrypted version.
Global Catalog (LDAPS) - Active Directory Global Catalog over TLS. Encrypted forest-wide AD queries across multiple domains.
FTPS Data - FTP over TLS/SSL data channel. The encrypted data transfer port for implicit FTPS. Used alongside port 990 (FTPS control).
FTPS Control - FTP over TLS/SSL control channel. Implicit FTPS (TLS negotiated immediately). Used with port 989 for data. Explicit FTPS uses STARTTLS on ports 20/21 instead.

RADIUS over TLS - RADIUS authentication wrapped in TLS (RadSec). Encrypts entire RADIUS exchange, not just password. Uses TCP for reliability. Useful for跨-network RADIUS proxying over untrusted networks (e.g., eduroam).
